neutral_facts.value: The accused, along with a co-accused, were present in the house on the day of the incident. The accused poured kerosene oil on his wife and set her on fire. The victim was taken to the hospital where she succumbed to burn injuries. The victim's brother lodged an FIR. A dying declaration was made by the victim in the presence of a doctor and a nurse, stating that her husband had set her on fire. The doctor and nurse's statements were corroborated by the victim's brother and another witness who accompanied him to the hospital. The prosecution case relied on the dying declaration, medical evidence, and eyewitness accounts to establish the accused's guilt.

prosecution_argument.value: The prosecution argued that the appellant-accused poured kerosene oil on his wife and set her on fire, leading to her death. The evidence included two dying declarations from the victim, corroborated by witnesses, and the victim's death was attributed to burn injuries.

quotes.text: The prosecution examined as many as seven witnesses
PW-8 had accompanied PW-1 to the hospital and deposed that the deceased had made a dying declaration in their presence stating that her husband had set her on fire
The trial court found the appellant guilty of the offence punishable under section 302 IPC

defence_argument.value: The defence argued that the dying declaration made by the victim was unreliable, as it was an oral statement and there was no smell of kerosene oil on the victim's body. They also cited the case of Surinder Kumar v. State of Haryana to challenge the admissibility of the dying declaration.

quotes.text: Mr. P.K. Goswami, learned Senior Counsel appearing for the appellant, assailed the impugned judgment and order of the High Court on two grounds
He firstly contends that no reliance can be placed upon Ex.6 i.e. the report prepared by Dr. Langkumer inasmuch as allegedly it was an oral dying declaration
He put reliance on the decision of this Court in the case of Surinder Kumar vs. State of Haryana - (2011) 10 SCC 173
He contends that there was no smell of kerosene oil from the body of the victim which falsifies the entire case of the prosecution

legal_principle_applied.value: The Supreme Court applied the principle that a dying declaration is admissible if it is corroborated by other evidence and the circumstances surrounding its making are not suspicious.

quotes.text: The statement of PW-6 Dr. Langkumer and PW-7 Nabanita Barauh that the victim made a dying declaration that her husband poured kerosene oil on her and set her on fire has been fully corroborated by PW-1 and PW-8
There is no evidence to the contrary that any effort was made by anyone to induce the deceased to make the false statement
Further absence of smell of kerosene oil in the hair of the deceased sent for chemical examination does not render the dying declaration doubtful and unbelievable
